notes.subtitle: Common Factors, Common Multiples, HCF & LCM

concepts.title: Listing method
concepts.text: Write the factors of each number and pick the largest common one: factors of 12 and 18 → common 1, 2, 3, 6 → HCF 6.

concepts.title: Prime factorisation method
concepts.text: Write each number as a product of primes. HCF = product of the common primes with the smaller powers. LCM = product of all primes with the larger powers.

concepts.title: HCF × LCM
concepts.text: For two numbers a and b: HCF × LCM = a × b. Use it to find a missing number.

concepts.title: HCF or LCM? Reading word problems
concepts.text: HCF: 'largest', 'greatest size', 'equal groups', 'tiles', 'boxes', 'cut into equal pieces'.

practice.question: Two numbers have HCF 4 and LCM 72. One is 24. Find the other.
Three ropes 64 m, 80 m, 96 m are cut into equal pieces of greatest length. Find the length and the number of pieces.
Traffic lights change every 48 s, 72 s and 108 s. They change together at 7:00 a.m. When next?

notes.intro: When two things share something in common, maths can find it. HCF finds the biggest equal group size; LCM finds when repeating events meet again. In this chapter you learn both, with quick methods and many real-life uses.

glossary.meaning: A number that divides another exactly. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
A number in the times table: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, …
Highest common factor: the largest number that divides all the given numbers.
Lowest common multiple: the smallest number that all the given numbers divide.
Two numbers whose HCF is 1, such as 8 and 15.

lessons.title: Listing method
text: Write the factors of each number and pick the largest common one: factors of 12 and 18 → common 1, 2, 3, 6 → HCF 6.
Write multiples and pick the smallest common one: multiples of 4 and 6 → 12, 24, … → LCM 12.

lessons.title: Prime factorisation method
text: Write each number as a product of primes. HCF = product of the common primes with the smaller powers. LCM = product of all primes with the larger powers.
points: HCF: common, smaller powers. LCM: all, larger powers.

lessons.title: HCF × LCM
text: For two numbers a and b: HCF × LCM = a × b. Use it to find a missing number.
Check: 8 and 12 → HCF 4, LCM 24, and 4 × 24 = 96 = 8 × 12.

lessons.title: HCF or LCM? Reading word problems
text: HCF: 'largest', 'greatest size', 'equal groups', 'tiles', 'boxes', 'cut into equal pieces'.
LCM: 'next time together', 'smallest number divisible by', 'bells', 'traffic lights', 'runners'.
For remainders: the smallest number leaving remainder r when divided by a, b, c is LCM(a, b, c) + r.
points: Largest piece → HCF. Next meeting → LCM.

examples.question: Largest square tile for 360 cm × 600 cm.
Smallest number leaving 2 when divided by 6, 8, 10.

mistakes: Using LCM for a 'largest size' question.
Taking larger powers for HCF.
Forgetting to add the remainder.
Using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers (it works only for two).
checklist: Write the prime factorisation in index form.
State HCF or LCM before calculating.
Answer in the units of the question.
Check that the HCF divides each number.

notes.subtitle: Multiplying & Dividing Decimals

concepts.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100, 1,000
concepts.text: × 10 moves the point 1 place right; × 100 moves it 2 places; × 1,000 moves it 3 places. Division moves it left in the same way.

concepts.title: Multiplying decimals
concepts.text: Multiply as if there were no points. Then count the total decimal places in both numbers, and put that many places in the answer.

concepts.title: Dividing decimals
concepts.text: Make the divisor a whole number: multiply both numbers by the same power of 10. 7.56 ÷ 1.8 = 75.6 ÷ 18 = 4.2.

concepts.title: Fractions to decimals
concepts.text: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3/8 = 0.375. Or make the denominator 10, 100 or 1,000: 7/20 = 35/100 = 0.35.

method: Place the decimal point by counting places.
For division, make the divisor whole first.

practice.question: A pen costs ₹7.75. Find the cost of 24 pens.
How many 0.25 L glasses from 7.5 L of juice?
A car uses 6.4 L of petrol for 89.6 km. Find the distance per litre and the petrol for 210 km.

notes.intro: In Chapter 3 you added and subtracted decimals. Now you multiply and divide them, as you do when you find the cost of 12.4 litres of petrol. You also learn why some fractions give decimals that end and others repeat forever.
before: know place value after the decimal point

glossary.meaning: The number of digits after the point. 2.35 has 2 decimal places.
A decimal that ends, such as 0.375.
A decimal in which a digit or group repeats forever, such as 0.333…

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100, 1,000
text: × 10 moves the point 1 place right; × 100 moves it 2 places; × 1,000 moves it 3 places. Division moves it left in the same way.
points: Count the zeros = places to move.

lessons.title: Multiplying decimals
text: Multiply as if there were no points. Then count the total decimal places in both numbers, and put that many places in the answer.
points: Total places in the question = places in the answer.

lessons.title: Dividing decimals
text: Make the divisor a whole number: multiply both numbers by the same power of 10. 7.56 ÷ 1.8 = 75.6 ÷ 18 = 4.2.
This does not change the answer, because both numbers grow by the same factor.
points: Move both points the same number of places.

lessons.title: Fractions to decimals
text: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3/8 = 0.375. Or make the denominator 10, 100 or 1,000: 7/20 = 35/100 = 0.35.
In lowest terms, if the denominator has only 2s and 5s as prime factors, the decimal terminates. Otherwise it repeats: 1/3 = 0.333…, 5/11 = 0.4545…

mistakes: Wrong number of decimal places in a product.
Moving the point in only one number when dividing.
Thinking every fraction gives a terminating decimal.
Not checking with an estimate.
checklist: Show the count of decimal places.
Write money to two places.
Use a bar for repeating digits if you can.

notes.subtitle: Statistical Questions, Mean, Median & Range

concepts.title: Statistical questions and statements
concepts.text: 'How tall is Ravi?' has one answer. 'How tall are the students of Class 7?' expects many different answers: it is a statistical question.

concepts.title: The mean
concepts.text: Add all the values and divide by how many there are. Mean of 2, 7, 9, 4, 3 = 25 ÷ 5 = 5.

concepts.title: The median
concepts.text: Arrange the data in order. If the count is odd, the median is the middle value. If it is even, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

concepts.title: Range and comparing data
concepts.text: Range = highest − lowest. A small range means the data are close together (consistent).

method: Find the sum and count for the mean.
Find the middle for the median.
Find max − min for the range, and interpret.

practice.question: Is 'What is your shoe size?' asked to the whole class a statistical question?
The mean of 6 numbers is 15. One number 30 is removed. Find the new mean.
Marks: 35, 40, 38, 95, 37. Which is better, mean or median? Find both.
Find x if the mean of 4, 7, x, 9 is 7.
Heights (cm): 142, 150, 138, 155, 147, 150. Find the mean, the median and the range.

notes.intro: Data are collections of numbers about the world: marks, prices, heights. In this chapter you learn to ask good statistical questions and to describe data with one 'representative value' (the mean or the median) and its spread (the range).
before: add and divide numbers, including decimals

glossary.meaning: A collection of numbers or facts.
A question whose answer depends on data that varies.
Sum of the values ÷ number of values.
The middle value after arranging the data in order.
Highest value − lowest value. It measures spread.

lessons.title: Statistical questions and statements
text: 'How tall is Ravi?' has one answer. 'How tall are the students of Class 7?' expects many different answers: it is a statistical question.
A statistical statement describes data, for example 'Most students in our class are between 140 cm and 150 cm tall.'

lessons.title: The mean
text: Add all the values and divide by how many there are. Mean of 2, 7, 9, 4, 3 = 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
If the mean and the number of values are known, total = mean × number. Use this to find a missing value.

example.question: The mean of five numbers is 12; four are 10, 14, 9, 15. Find the fifth.

lessons.title: The median
text: Arrange the data in order. If the count is odd, the median is the middle value. If it is even, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
The median is not affected much by one very large or very small value, so it is often better than the mean for such data.

lessons.title: Range and comparing data
text: Range = highest − lowest. A small range means the data are close together (consistent).
To compare two groups, compare their means (or medians) and their ranges. A dot plot shows each value as a dot above a number line.

examples.question: Mean of five is 12; four are 10, 14, 9, 15.

mistakes: Finding the median without ordering.
Taking only one middle value for an even count.
Dividing by the wrong count for the mean.
Calling range the highest value.
checklist: Write the ordered list.
Show the sum and the count.
State which value is better and why.
Give units.

notes.subtitle: Compass Constructions & Tessellations

concepts.title: Perpendicular bisector
concepts.text: Open the compasses to more than half of AB. Draw arcs above and below AB from A, then from B with the same radius. Join the two crossing points.

concepts.title: Angles of 60°, 30°, 90° and 45°
concepts.text: 60°: from the vertex, draw an arc; from where it cuts the arm, cut the arc again with the same radius. Join.

concepts.title: Parallel line through a point
concepts.text: Draw any line through P that crosses l. Copy the angle that it makes with l at P, in the corresponding position. The equal corresponding angles make the new line parallel to l.

concepts.title: Which shapes tile?
concepts.text: At each corner of a tiling, the angles must add to exactly 360°.

method: For tilings, add the angles at a point.

example.question: Steps for the perpendicular bisector of AB.
steps: Equal arcs from A and B above and below.

practice.question: Interior angle of a regular pentagon.
How many squares meet at a point in a tiling?
Bisect a 90° angle. What angle do you get?
Do 1 square + 2 octagons fit at a point?
Do 3 triangles + 2 squares fit at a point?
Show that 1 triangle + 2 dodecagons (150°) fit at a point.

tips: Fixed radius for each pair of arcs.
Tiles must total 360° at a corner.
notes.intro: With only a ruler and compasses, you can draw exact right angles, 60° angles and parallel lines. In this chapter you learn these constructions and then use angle facts to see which tile shapes can cover a floor without gaps.
before: know the angle sum of a triangle and that angles round a point add to 360°

glossary.meaning: A line at 90° through the mid-point of a segment.
A ray that splits an angle into two equal parts.
All sides equal and all angles equal.
Covering a surface with shapes, without gaps or overlaps.

lessons.title: Perpendicular bisector
text: Open the compasses to more than half of AB. Draw arcs above and below AB from A, then from B with the same radius. Join the two crossing points.
Every point on this line is the same distance from A and B.

lessons.title: Angles of 60°, 30°, 90° and 45°
text: 60°: from the vertex, draw an arc; from where it cuts the arm, cut the arc again with the same radius. Join.
Bisect any angle: from the two points where an arc cuts the arms, draw equal arcs inside; join the vertex to their crossing point. Bisect 60° for 30°, 90° for 45°.
points: Keep the compass width fixed during each step.

lessons.title: Parallel line through a point
text: Draw any line through P that crosses l. Copy the angle that it makes with l at P, in the corresponding position. The equal corresponding angles make the new line parallel to l.

lessons.title: Which shapes tile?
text: At each corner of a tiling, the angles must add to exactly 360°.
Interior angle of a regular polygon with n sides = 180° × (n − 2) ÷ n. Triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°, octagon 135°.
Only regular triangles, squares and hexagons tile alone. Mixtures also work if the angles at a point add to 360°.

examples.question: Steps for the perpendicular bisector of AB.
steps: Equal arcs from A and B above and below.

examples.question: Interior angle of a regular octagon.
Line through P parallel to l.
steps: Copy the corresponding angle at P.

mistakes: Changing the compass width in the middle of a step.
Erasing construction arcs.
Using 180°(n − 2) without dividing by n.
Forgetting that angles at a point must total exactly 360°.
checklist: Keep arcs visible.
Write the steps of construction.
Show the 360° check for tilings.
Measure angles with a protractor to check.

notes.subtitle: Simple Linear Equations

concepts.title: The balance idea
concepts.text: An equation stays true if you add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number (not dividing by 0).

concepts.title: Brackets and unknowns on both sides
concepts.text: Expand brackets first, or divide both sides by the number outside: 5(y − 2) = 30 → y − 2 = 6 → y = 8.

concepts.title: Checking a solution
concepts.text: Put the value back into the original equation. If both sides are equal, the solution is correct.

concepts.title: Word problems
concepts.text: Step 1: let a letter stand for the unknown. Step 2: write the other quantities using that letter. Step 3: form the equation from the condition. Step 4: solve and check. Step 5: answer in words with units.

formulas: If a = b, then a + c = b + c, a − c = b − c, ac = bc, a/c = b/c (c ≠ 0)
method: Let the unknown be a letter.

practice.question: The sum of three consecutive numbers is 72. Find them.
A father is 30 years older than his son. In 5 years he will be 3 times as old. Find the son's age.
I think of a number, multiply it by 5 and subtract 12. I get 48. Find the number.
₹500 is shared between A and B so that A gets ₹80 more than B. Find each share.

notes.intro: An equation is like a balance: both sides weigh the same. To find the unknown number, you do the same thing to both sides until the letter is alone. In this chapter you learn to solve equations and to turn word problems into equations.

glossary.meaning: A statement that two expressions are equal, such as 2x + 9 = 35.
The letter whose value we want.
The value that makes the equation true.
The left-hand side and the right-hand side of the = sign.

lessons.title: The balance idea
text: An equation stays true if you add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number (not dividing by 0).
Undo operations in reverse order: in 3x + 4 = 25, first subtract 4, then divide by 3.
points: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

lessons.title: Brackets and unknowns on both sides
text: Expand brackets first, or divide both sides by the number outside: 5(y − 2) = 30 → y − 2 = 6 → y = 8.
If x appears on both sides, move the x terms to one side and the numbers to the other: 4x − 7 = 2x + 9 → 2x = 16 → x = 8.

lessons.title: Checking a solution
text: Put the value back into the original equation. If both sides are equal, the solution is correct.
Check x = 8 in 4x − 7 = 2x + 9: LHS = 25, RHS = 25. Correct.

lessons.title: Word problems
text: Step 1: let a letter stand for the unknown. Step 2: write the other quantities using that letter. Step 3: form the equation from the condition. Step 4: solve and check. Step 5: answer in words with units.
Common forms: perimeter 2(l + b); ages now and after n years; costs 'more than' or 'less than'.

mistakes: Doing an operation on one side only.
Forgetting to multiply every term inside a bracket.
Sign errors when moving terms.
Not answering the actual question (for example giving b, when the length is asked).
checklist: Write 'Let … = x'.
Write each step on a new line.
Check by substitution.
Give units.
